opus-5.5.text:
I think the core difference is generalization. Traditional industrial robots, even the ones with 3D vision, are basically operating in a structured world. Someone engineered the station, fixed the fixtures, defined the parts, and the vision system is there to compensate for small deviations: find the pose of a known object, compute a grasp, then execute a pre-programmed trajectory. The intelligence is mostly in the human engineers who set up the cell. If you change the product, change the lighting, or throw in an object it has never seen, you often need to re-tune or re-program the whole thing.

What we're trying to build with embodied, physical agents is different in kind, not just degree. We want a system that can perceive an open, unstructured environment, understand what it's looking at semantically, and then decide how to act, closing the loop continuously. So it's not "detect, plan once, execute blindly," but perceive, act, observe the result, and adjust, much more like how a person does it. And crucially, it should handle novel objects, novel scenes, and novel instructions without someone rewriting code for every case.

To get there, the technical stack changes a lot. In the old paradigm, 3D vision was a module, a measurement tool. In our paradigm, perception, reasoning, and control are increasingly learned together, models that take in vision and language and output actions. And the bottleneck shifts from algorithms to data: how do you get enough high-quality, diverse interaction data to train a generalist? That's why we put so much emphasis on things like large-scale synthetic data and simulation, because collecting real-world teleoperation data alone is too slow and expensive to reach the scale you need for real generalization.

So, in one sentence: the old industrial robot is an automated tool for a fixed task, while a physical intelligent agent aims to be a general-purpose worker that can adapt to the world rather than requiring the world to be adapted to it. That shift from specialized to general is, to me, exactly what makes this moment in robotics so exciting.

fable-5.1.text:
I think the core difference comes down to one word: generalization.

Traditional industrial robots with 3D vision are, at heart, programmed systems. You put a camera on the arm, you calibrate it to a fixed workcell, you teach it the exact part, the exact pose, the exact grasp. If the part changes, if the lighting changes, if someone moves the bin ten centimeters, an engineer has to go in and re-tune it. The 3D vision gives it eyes, but the "brain" behind the eyes is a set of hand-written rules. It perceives, but it doesn't really understand. It works beautifully in a structured, closed environment, which is why automotive lines and electronics factories have used it for decades. But it's essentially one robot, one task, one scene.

What we're building is different in kind, not just in degree. A physical intelligent agent is driven by a learned model, a foundation model for the body, if you like. Instead of writing rules, we train it on large amounts of data: simulation data, real-world interaction data, human demonstrations. The goal is that when it encounters an object it has never seen, in a kitchen or warehouse it has never been in, it can still reason about what the object is, how to grasp it, what will happen if it pushes it, and how to recover when the grasp fails.

So the three things I'd point to are, first, open-world perception, meaning it handles novel objects and cluttered scenes rather than a pre-registered part library. Second, closed-loop decision-making, where it continuously perceives and adjusts, rather than executing a pre-planned trajectory and hoping nothing changed. And third, transfer: the same model and skills carry across different robot bodies and different tasks, so capability accumulates instead of being rebuilt from scratch for each deployment.

To put it simply, the old industrial robot is a very precise tool. What we want is something closer to a worker: you can give it a new task in language, drop it into a new environment, and it figures out how to do the job. We're not fully there yet, and honestly, a lot of our work is about closing the data gap between language models and physical skills. But that's the direction, and that's the fundamental distinction.

astra-6.text:
I think the key difference is whether the robot is executing a predefined process or can understand a task and adapt its actions to the situation.

An industrial robot with 3D vision can already do useful things: locate a part, estimate its pose, and adjust a grasp. But usually, people have defined the objects it will encounter, the steps it should follow, and how to handle exceptions. Vision makes that process more flexible, but adding a camera doesn’t by itself change the underlying approach.

For a physical intelligent agent, we want perception, decision-making, and action to form a continuous loop. If you ask it to clear a table, it needs to work out what to move, how to grasp each object, and where to put it. If something slips or an object is obstructed, it should use that feedback to adjust what it does next.

Of course, this is a direction we’re working toward, not a claim that robots can already handle every unfamiliar situation. Traditional industrial robots are extremely good at speed, precision, and repeatability. The additional capability we’re pursuing is generalization: how much of what a robot has learned can it carry into a new task or environment without someone having to engineer the whole process again?

sol-6.1.text:
I think the key difference is whether the robot is executing a predefined process or can perceive, decide, and act as the situation changes. Adding 3D vision to an industrial robot gives it more information, but the overall workflow can still be fixed: identify a part, estimate its pose, and execute a programmed motion. That works very well when the task and environment are tightly controlled.

For a physical intelligent agent, perception and action have to form a continuous loop. If an object moves, a grasp slips, or something unexpected happens, the robot needs to use that feedback to adjust what it does next. It also needs to apply what it has learned to unfamiliar objects and situations, rather than requiring someone to program every variation.

So I wouldn’t draw the boundary at whether a robot has 3D vision. The question is how much of the task’s intelligence comes from engineers anticipating every condition, and how much the robot itself can handle through learning and interaction with the physical world.
